faqs.question: How many non-candy treats should I buy for Halloween night?
faqs.answer: Without a count from last year, start with about 50 items split across a toddler bowl and a main bowl, roughly $15 to $30 EST. Non-food items do not go stale, so anything left over keeps until Sunday 31 October 2027.

faqs.question: Can I put toys and candy in the same bowl?
faqs.answer: Keep them apart. A toy that has sat among loose chocolate can pick up traces of milk or peanut, which defeats the point for an allergic child. Hold the toy bowl at the door and leave the candy on a table behind you.

faqs.question: What can I give a baby or toddler who comes trick-or-treating?
faqs.answer: Hand something to the parent that is labelled 0+ and too big to swallow, such as a silicone teether or a wipe-clean colouring placemat. Avoid anything with a cap, a battery or a part that could be bitten off.

faqs.question: Is fruit a good alternative to Halloween candy?
faqs.answer: Only if it is shop-sealed, such as an apple purée pouch or a bag of freeze-dried fruit. Many parents throw away anything unwrapped from a stranger's door, so loose apples or clementines are usually wasted.

faqs.question: Is sugar-free candy a good choice for a child with diabetes?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Children with type 1 diabetes can usually eat ordinary candy with insulin, and families often keep some to treat lows with 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate. A non-food item is the simpler choice because it needs no dosing decision at all.

faqs.question: What do teenagers want instead of Halloween candy?
faqs.answer: Things they would buy themselves: a die-cut laptop sticker, an enamel pin or a printed screen cloth, at about $0.30 to $1.00 EST each. Anything that looks like a toddler toy gets left on the wall outside.

faqs.question: Why do some houses put out a teal pumpkin?
faqs.answer: A teal pumpkin tells families that this house keeps a bowl of non-food items, so a child with a food allergy can join in. The idea comes from the US charity FARE's Teal Pumpkin Project, and any house can take part by putting out a teal pumpkin and a non-food bowl.

faqs.question: Are coins a good thing to hand out on Halloween?
faqs.answer: Only to older children. Common coins fit inside the federal small-parts test cylinder, so a coin in a toddler's bag is a choking risk. For ages 10 and up, a single coin is a popular, compact treat.

faqs.question: Where can I buy non-candy Halloween treats cheaply?
faqs.answer: Party-supply multipacks of 24 to 144 pieces bring the price down to about $0.15 to $0.60 EST per item. Buy by early October, since Halloween ranges thin out in the final week, and check each pack's age label.

faqs.question: Is there a Halloween treat I can send a grandchild in another city?
faqs.answer: A parcel needs days to arrive, but a Halloween page arrives the moment you send the link. SubhSandesh's Halloween card has a Kids tone with no gore or jump scares, and a parent should open it with a young child.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Candy Alternatives to Hand Out, Sorted by Age and Cost

The best Halloween candy alternatives for a front door are non-food items you sort by the age of the child holding the bag: a teether-grade toy for a toddler on a hip, something to do for ages 6 to 9, and something a teenager would not be embarrassed to pocket. Budget about $0.15 to $1.20 per item (EST, typical US multipack prices), and never mix them into the candy. Children do not mind: in a 284-child porch study, kids aged 3 to 14 picked toys as often as sweets.

For the one child you cannot reach at the door, a link works too. Across 57,456 views of SubhSandesh pages, 48.3% were opened on a phone, and 90.9% of started pages get published. Below: 22 picks by age, a cost table, the US small-parts test, and the allergy, diabetes and sensory angles.

## What are non-candy Halloween treats, and do kids actually want them?

A non-candy Halloween treat is anything handed to a trick-or-treater in place of sweets: usually a small toy or stationery item, sometimes a shop-sealed food that is not candy. The point is that every child at the door gets something, whatever they can eat.

The evidence that children accept the swap comes from a short 2003 paper by Schwartz, Chen and Brownell in the *Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior* (volume 35, pages 207 to 209). Seven households offered 284 trick-or-treaters a choice between comparably sized toys and candies, and children were just as likely to choose a toy, with no difference between boys and girls. The journal is an Elsevier title and no open copy exists, so we read only the abstract and do not link it.

## 22 Halloween candy alternatives by age, with EST cost per item

Each pick gives the item, its EST unit price from a 20-to-50-pack, and why it suits that age. Judge age by height and by whether a parent is carrying the child.

### 1. Under 3, carried by a parent: 3 picks

Hand these to the adult. Each is bigger than any mouth, with nothing that snaps off.

- **Silicone pumpkin teether labelled 0+:** $1.00 to $1.40 EST; designed to be chewed, so it is the one item here a baby is meant to mouth.
- **Wipe-clean ghost colouring placemat:** $0.50 EST; one flat sheet, no parts.
- **Fabric crinkle square with a bat print:** $0.90 EST; sewn seams only, and it keeps small hands busy on the walk home.

### 2. Ages 3 to 5: 4 picks

Preschoolers want something to use that evening. Check each packet says 3+.

- **Two sticks of pavement chalk, orange and purple:** $0.30 EST; the front path becomes a ghost gallery.
- **Mini bottle of bubbles with a wand:** $0.25 EST; screw the cap tight before it goes in the bowl.
- **One sheet of monster-print plasters:** $0.20 EST; preschoolers treat a novelty plaster as a prize.
- **Squeezable foam ghost, 2.5 inches tall:** $0.35 EST; soft enough for a pillowcase bag.

### 3. Ages 6 to 9: 5 picks

This age trades and tests everything. A gadget beats a trinket.

- **Plastic magnifier with a bug-hunter card:** $0.40 EST; the garden becomes a crime scene.
- **Handheld water ring-toss game:** $0.50 EST; old-fashioned and still the first to go.
- **Scratch-to-reveal secret-message card:** $0.30 EST; they can write one back to a sibling.
- **Mini plastic coil spring in Halloween colours:** $0.35 EST; stairs become a racetrack.
- **Tasselled bookmark with a black cat:** $0.15 EST; the cheapest pick here, and it lives in a school book.

### 4. Ages 10 to 13: 4 picks

Tweens reject anything babyish. Pick things adults also own.

- **Pocket deck of monster card games:** $0.75 EST; two players, no batteries.
- **Two-piece wire brain-teaser:** $0.60 EST; frustrating in the right way, solvable in an evening.
- **Black gel pen with orange ink:** $0.40 EST; it stays in a pencil case for months.
- **Glow-in-the-dark shoelaces:** $0.50 EST; a visible kid on a dark street is a safer kid.

### 5. Teens, 13 and up: 3 picks

Teens often arrive in a group wearing little more than a hat. Give them something they would have chosen.

- **Die-cut vinyl laptop sticker with a skull:** $0.30 EST; laptops and water bottles are where teens display taste.
- **Microfibre screen cloth printed with bats:** $0.40 EST; useful on day one.
- **Enamel pin, crescent moon or ghost:** $1.00 EST; the priciest pick, so keep a short stack for the oldest callers.

### 6. Shop-sealed foods that are not candy: 3 picks

For something edible, keep the seal on. Read the label first.

- **Squeeze pouch of apple purée:** $0.40 EST; check the allergen line, and it suits younger children best.
- **Snack bag of freeze-dried strawberries:** $0.60 EST; light, crunchy, no added sugar on many brands.
- **Roasted chickpea snack pack:** $0.55 EST; chickpeas are a legume, so ask about legume allergies before handing it out.

## Candy alternatives compared by age, cost and main risk

This table summarises the five age groups above. Costs are EST per item, with the risk to plan for at the door.

| Age group | Strongest pick | EST cost per item | Main risk to manage |
|---|---|---|---|
| Under 3 | Silicone teether, 0+ | $1.00 to $1.40 | Anything under the federal 36-month test |
| 3 to 5 | Pavement chalk, 2 sticks | $0.20 to $0.35 | Bubble liquid spills, loose caps |
| 6 to 9 | Water ring-toss game | $0.15 to $0.50 | Trading with younger siblings at home |
| 10 to 13 | Card-game deck | $0.40 to $0.75 | Looking babyish, so ignored |
| 13 and up | Enamel pin | $0.30 to $1.00 | Teens arrive late, after stock runs low |

The takeaway: a 100-child night costs about $25 to $60 EST in non-food items. Only the toddler bowl needs real care.

## How the US small-parts test applies to a Halloween bowl

The US rule is in [16 CFR 1501.4](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-II/subchapter-C/part-1501/section-1501.4), which bars toys meant for children under 3 years (36 months) from fitting wholly inside the government's test cylinder. The cylinder test is run twice: once on the whole item, and again on every piece that breaks off after "use and abuse" testing. Paper, fabric, yarn, fuzz, elastic and string are excluded from that second test.

The second step matters at home: a foam ghost may pass whole and fail once a child bites off an ear, so tug and twist one sample before buying 50. Any item with a coin-cell battery goes only to older children, and only when a screw holds its compartment closed.

## Why Halloween is a peanut-risk night, and what to hand out instead

Food allergy is common enough that one child in most groups of trick-or-treaters has one. A US household survey covering 38,408 children, [published in Pediatrics in 2018](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC6317772), put childhood food allergy at 7.6%, with peanut at 2.2% and milk at 1.9%; 39.9% of allergic children had more than one.

Halloween shows up in emergency data. A [2020 CMAJ study of 1,390 Canadian children](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC7532006) seen for anaphylaxis between 2011 and 2020 found the mean daily count of peanut-triggered cases rose 85% at Halloween (incidence rate ratio 1.86) against the rest of the year. The rise was concentrated in children aged 6 and older, and the authors note individually sold one-bite snacks are exempt from Canadian allergen labelling.

A non-food bowl removes the label problem, while "allergy-friendly" candy only covers the allergens on its pack. The Teal Pumpkin Project, run by the US charity FARE, is the best-known way to signal that you have one: a teal pumpkin on the step means non-food items are available. Its history and sign-up are a separate topic; the practical part is the second bowl.

## Diabetes, dental and sensory needs: what to put in the bowl

For a child with type 1 diabetes, candy is partly medicine. A [2024 review in Clinical Diabetes](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC11486860) gives the standard treatment for a low as 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, with blood glucose rechecked 15 minutes later. Many families keep candy for that job, so a non-food item lets the child fill a bag without adding to the stash parents must count.

For teeth, a sticker or a pen has no sugar to brush off, which matters on a night when one bag can hold dozens of pieces. That is the whole dental case, and it is enough.

For autistic children or anyone sensitive to noise and light, pick quiet, unscented items with no flashing LEDs, such as the bookmark or magnifier. Lower the bowl to child height and let them choose without saying "trick or treat"; some children do not speak.

## The one child you can't reach at the door: a Halloween page

Some children you most want to treat are a flight away. A toy cannot reach a grandchild by 31 October (Saturday in 2026, Sunday in 2027), but a link can, and 27,725 of the 57,456 recorded views of SubhSandesh pages came from a phone.

The [interactive Halloween card for a child](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) takes about 5 minutes: up to 6 photos, a pumpkin they carve, and a Kids tone that is spooky-cute, with no gore and no jump scares, where the No button waits as "maybe later?". It ends with a Boo License sized 1080×1920, ready to download.

Choose the [Halloween page with a voice note](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) when you would rather the child hear you: a voice note up to 60 seconds, up to 12 photos, an optional unlock time and one reply box, and for family and kids the No button never appears. It takes about 10 minutes. For a birthday or another occasion, [browse every SubhSandesh template](https://subhsandesh.in/templates).

It is the wrong choice for trick-or-treaters on your street, for any party, and for a child under about 6 who cannot open a link alone; a parent has to sit with them. The interface is English only. And 38.5% of creators password-protect their page, which adds one more thing a young child must type.

## Sources

- [Gupta et al., childhood food allergy prevalence, Pediatrics](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC6317772), 19 November 2018.
- [Leung et al., holiday nut anaphylaxis in Canadian children, CMAJ](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC7532006), 21 September 2020.
- [Goldman and Isaacs, treating hypoglycemia, Clinical Diabetes](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC11486860), 14 August 2024.
- [16 CFR 1501.4, small-parts size test (eCFR)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-II/subchapter-C/part-1501/section-1501.4), current text read October 2026.
- SubhSandesh first-party data, measured 24 September 2026.
